abstract_text: Influence of environmental factors on prey discrimination of bait-attracted white sharks were studied over a six-year period (2008-2013) at Dyer Island Nature Reserve (Gansbaai, South Africa). This work deepens previous published study on surface predatory behaviour of bait-attracted white sharks conducted in the same area where, from 240 predator-prey interactions observed in the same period, both immature and mature white sharks were attracted from the seal shaped decoy rather than the tuna bait, except for the years 2008 and 2011. Tide ranges, underwater visibility, water temperature, and sea conditions are, in decreasing order, the factors that drive white sharks to the prey choice. High tide reduces the minimum depth from which sharks could approach seals close to the shore, while a good visibility helps the sharks to use their vision ability to implement predatory choices to energetical richer prey, the odorless seal shaped decoy. On the contrary, warmer water is associated both with an increasing and diversity of teleosts which are prey of white sharks and to an increase of phytoplankton that reduces the underwater visibility, driving them to the tuna bait choice. Finally, sea condition was almost always slightly rough, ensuring a good average underwater visibility. Recommendations for future research work at this site are presented.

abstract_text: Many elasmobranchs exhibit complex courtship rituals. The function of large aggregations of basking sharks engaged in circling behaviour largely remains a mystery. We present, underwater and aerial video recordings of multiple circling groups of basking sharks in late summer (August to September) during years 2016–2021 in Ireland. Groups comprised females and males numbering between 6 and 23 individuals that were not filter feeding. Grouped sharks swam slowly in a clockwise or anticlockwise rotating ‘torus’ (diameter range: 17–39 m) consisting of circling individuals layered vertically from the surface to a maximum depth of 16 m. Within a torus, sharks engaged in close-following, echelon, close flank-approach or parallel swimming behaviours. Total body lengths of circling sharks overlapped known lengths of sexually mature individuals. In some toruses female body coloration was paler than that of males. Within a torus individuals associated with most other members rapidly (within minutes) indicating toroidal behaviours facilitate multiple interactions. Torus members also interacted through fin-fin and fin-body contacts, rolling to expose ventral surfaces to following sharks, and breaching behaviour. We also confirmed that a torus forms from shark following behaviour, and can change rotation direction frequently. Collectively, our observations explain a courtship function for non-feeding circling groups. This study highlights the importance of coastal waters off western Ireland as critical habitats supporting courtship reproductive behaviour of endangered basking sharks, the first such habitats identified for this species globally. This has important conservation implications for a species recently given legal protection status in Ireland.

abstract_text: White shark movements are typically observed over large spatial scales (100s-1000s km2). However, observation of fine-scale movement behaviour of white sharks is necessary to improve our understanding of their usage of near-shore coastal areas where there is an increased probability of interactions between sharks and humans. Based on passive acoustic data from a dense, but non-triangulating, array we investigated the fine scale movement of white sharks at a coastal beach within a nursery area off Hawk’s Nest, New South Wales from 2010-2015. Using a spatial Hidden Markov Model (HMM) we were able to estimate white shark movement tracks during each shark visit to the array based on detection binning over 5-minute time intervals. The HMM also enabled direct estimation of the probability of detection as a function of distance from shark to acoustic receivers. The HMM-estimated movement tracks predict heavy utilisation of very shallow water close to the high-water mark by the sharks. Additionally, the southern end of the beach appears to be a focus for short term white shark residency at the beach. The movement tracks estimated here allowed the first high-resolution investigation of white shark movements in the Hawk’s Nest nursery area and demonstrate the potential for estimation of fine-scale position data from non-triangulating passive acoustic monitoring arrays deployed in other coastal marine areas.

title: Making a Difference: how to realize policy change

authors.affiliation: Irish Basking Shark Group; George Mason University
Irish Basking Shark Group; Queen's University Belfast; National Parks and Wildlife Service

abstract_text: Shark research and conservation efforts are typically driven by a desire to inform the status assessment and increase the level of protection afforded to the target species. However, the translation of scientific findings and or conservation initiatives into real world policy change is a persistent challenge for non-governmental organisations and academics. Basking sharks are listed by the IUCN as globally endangered. Ireland is significant to basking sharks in the Northeast Atlantic, however until 2022, they were not protected under domestic legislation. To help others overcome this disconnect we describe and review the methods that the Irish Basking Shark Group (IBSG), a volunteer research and outreach organisation, deployed to realize a change in legislative status for the species in Irish waters. Between 2009 and 2022 the IBSG delivered approximately forty research, outreach and legislative change initiatives designed to raise the awareness, understanding and appreciation of basking sharks in Irish and International waters. No individual action or effort stream (i.e., public outreach, scientific research or political lobbying) delivered alone. Rather an integrated approach that melded internationally significant research studies with locally orientated ocean literacy initiates’ and strategically timed media campaigns provided the maximum leverage of policy makers. Lastly, we consider how these experiences can be applied to other species or scaled up to regional forums. Our goal here is to provide a road map for similar conservation efforts through sharing our experience in attaining protection for the basking shark in Irish wildlife legislation, the first fish to be given this status.

title: Capture heats up sharks
abstract_text: Catch-and-release fishing is an important component of ecotourism industries and scientific research worldwide, but its total impact on animal physiology, health and survival is understudied for many species of sharks. We combined biologging and blood chemistry to explore how this fisheries interaction influenced the physiology of two widely distributed, highly migratory shark species: blue sharks (Prionace glauca), and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier). Nineteen sharks were caught by drum line or rod-and-reel angling; subcutaneous body temperature measurements were taken immediately upon capture, with 6 individuals also providing subsequent subcutaneous body temperature measurements via biologging as they swam freely for several hours post-release. We found that short-term capture caused shark body temperature to increase significantly and rapidly, with increases of 0.6 – 2.7°C for blue sharks (mean 1.2 ± 0.6°C) and 0.5 – 0.9°C for tiger sharks (mean 0.7 ± 0.2°C), and with capture-induced heating rates of blue sharks averaging 0.3°C min-1 but as high as 0.8°C min-1. These heating rates were 3-8 times faster than maximum rates encountered by our biologging sharks swimming through thermally stratified waters. Biologging data showed that body temperatures underwent gradual decline after release, returning to match water temperatures approximately 10 – 40 mins post-release. Blood biochemistry showed variable lactate/glucose levels following capture; however, these concentrations weren’t correlated with the magnitude of body temperature increase, nor body size or hooking time. These perturbations of the natural state could have immediate and longer-term effects on the welfare and ecology of sharks caught and future research could focus on exploring these effects.

title: The recreational shore-based shark fishery in Florida, USA; catch rates, mortality rates and updates
abstract_text: Recreational, rod and reel, shore-based shark fishing is a popular activity along the coast of Florida, USA. The recent review of NOAA’s recreational fishing data resulted in a six-fold increase in the estimation of effort, catch and harvest by all shore-based anglers. A portion of these data are collected in part by intercepting anglers at fishing access points, however, it may not capture those involved in shore-based shark fishing which occurs mostly at night in locations with relative low fishing activity. We analyzed responses to our online survey of Florida shore-based shark fishing permit holders representing a subset that specifically target great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran) to better describe angler demographics, motivations, gear types, and behaviors. We will also present survivorship data on the great hammerheads caught and released with pop-off archival satellite tags (PSATs) to estimate the post-release mortality rates of this species in the shore-based fishery and insights into the diversity of species caught in this fishery, including several species with upcoming stock assessments. These data, both the human dimension and the mortality rates, are important to decision-makers for calculating Annual Catch Limits across the commercial and recreational sectors as well as provide evidence for the development of best practices for the angling community.

title: Stress indicators in deep-sea sharks from bottom trawl fisheries in Southern Portugal

authors.affiliation: Portuguese Institute of the Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA)

abstract_text: Crustacean bottom-trawlers are responsible for 70% of discards in the south of Portugal and deep-sea sharks are expressive bycatch, due to their overlap with fishing grounds, low commercial values and/or fishing regulations. Most individuals are discarded either dead or in poor physical condition. The physiological consequences of this type of capture in elasmobranchs are poorly understood. This study analyzed stress-related physiological parameters of four common deep-sea shark, sampled from two different trawling procedures: one conducted onboard a commercial crustacean bottom-trawler (longer haul duration and heavier codend weight) and the other conducted onboard a research vessel (shorter haul duration and lighter codend weight). A total of 120 individuals from the species Etmopterus pusillus, Etmopterus spinax, Galeus melastomus and Scymnodon ringens were studied. Plasma was collected onboard and frozen until analysis. The concentrations (mmol/L) of plasma electrolytes (Na+, Cl-, Ca2+, Mg2+) and energy metabolites (glucose, lactate) were measured and related to specific trawling conditions, specimen vitality and survival. Differences between commercial and research hauls were observed. Commercial hauls were marked by significantly high concentrations of Na+, Cl-, Mg2+ and lactate, whilst research hauls presented higher concentrations of glucose and Ca2+. Specifically, commercial hauls caused significant increases in Cl- and lactate for S. ringens and Na+ for E. pusillus, and a decrease in glucose concentrations for E. pusillus. A complete analysis of the relation between physiological stress indicators and trawling variables should provide further insight to establish additional recommendations to increase the welfare and the effective management of discarded deep-sea sharks.

abstract_text: Pelagic sharks are highly threatened by overfishing and in urgent need of science-based conservation management. A key need is improved information on the population genetic structure and diversity of these ecologically important taxa. The shortfin mako shark (Isurus oxyrinchus) is an oceanic, globally widespread species known for its capacity for long-distance movements spanning thousands of kilometers. This species is listed as globally ‘Endangered’ by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and Atlantic makos are considered overfished and in decline. We investigated the population genetic dynamics of shortfin mako sharks in the Atlantic Ocean using a high-resolution, bi-organelle, multi-marker, genomics approach. We sequenced 86 complete mitochondrial genomes (mitogenomes) (16,999-17,002 bp) and genotyped 4236 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in 105 sharks across the Atlantic and found contrasting patterns of genetic population structure across DNA markers. Mitogenome sequences indicated matrilineal population genetic structure across northern and southern hemispheres, while nuclear-based SNPs showed high connectivity and ocean basin-wide panmixia. Mitogenome genetic diversity in Atlantic shortfin makos was high compared to other elasmobranchs assessed at the population mitogenome level, and nuclear diversity was high compared to migratory shark species assessed with SNP markers, boding well for the genetic recovery of Atlantic shortfin makos if further population declines can be halted.

title: Accelerated progress in global shark research and conservation by OCEARCH
abstract_text: Since 2007, OCEARCH has conducted 44 expeditions in nine countries focusing on comprehensive research and public awareness of sharks and other marine vertebrates. Our goal is to provide the data to return balance, abundance, and ecological health to our oceans, starting with rebuilding populations of its top predators. By donating the unique facilities, capabilities, and skilled crew of our 40m research ship to the scientific community at no cost, OCEARCH provides unprecedented access to large sharks in the wild for advanced studies of their biology, conservation status, and human impacts. Using the Google business model to build and monetize scale, we follow these principles to advance shark research: 1) broad collaboration, uniting fishermen, scientists, educators, and policymakers to rapidly increase our knowledge on sharks; 2) the 3Rs of animal research, minimizing the number of sharks needed to answer the maximum number of questions, while ensuring the health and safety of each shark studied; 3) inclusion, allowing the world to participate in real time through open access to new scientific data; and 4) innovative funding, from brand-integrated content, conscious consumerism, and philanthropy. OCEARCH has facilitated the work of more than 200 scientists in the Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans, resulting in 75 peer-reviewed publications, and we have advanced public awareness through our Global Shark TrackerTM app and website, social media, and STEM educational programs. With our multi-year study of the white shark in the Western North Atlantic completed, we are bringing our ship to Europe and the Mediterranean in 2023.

title: Across the Pond: White shark research from the Western North Atlantic to Europe and the Mediterranean Sea
abstract_text: With the completion of a multi-year comprehensive study of white shark biology in the Western North Atlantic (WNA) by OCEARCH and its collaborators, knowledge of the WNA population has rapidly surpassed the level previously attained in Australia and New Zealand, South Africa, and the eastern Pacific. A total of 19 expeditions along the North American Atlantic coast have supported the multidisciplinary work of 45 investigators from 30 organizations to advance 25 individual research projects. By maximizing the number of projects served and minimizing the handling stress for each individual shark, we applied the principles of Reduction and Refinement to study spatial ecology and behavior, reproduction, trophic ecology, environmental health and physiology, population genetics, microbiology and biomedicine, and more aspects of WNA white sharks. Results include a comprehensive understanding of the life history, critical habitats, and threats to YOY, juvenile, subadult, and adult white sharks in the WNA, where the population is currently rebuilding. We next turn our attention and resources to the white shark population of the Eastern North Atlantic (ENA) and Mediterranean Sea, where studies of white sharks have been largely restricted to fisheries records and anecdotal observations, indicating a declining population. In 17 ENA and Mediterranean countries to date, we have established a network of 70 researchers from 55 organizations to collaborate in OCEARCH expeditions in 2023-2025. Focal regions of study will include Scotland, Ireland, England, and France, the western Mediterranean including Malta and Tunisia, and the eastern Mediterranean including the Aegean and Adriatic Seas.

title: Western North Atlantic white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) baseline health assessment and plasma one-alpha hydroxycorticosterone response during scientific sampling, tagging, and release

authors.affiliation: University of Florida, School of Veterinary Medicine
Wildlife Conservation Society, New York Aquarium
South Fork Natural History Museum and Nature Center

abstract_text: Health assessments in wildlife populations are essential to understanding individual animal, in situ population, and ecosystem health in the face of current and future natural and anthropogenic environmental disturbance. Creating species specific baselines for health comparisons is a critical need across all elasmobranch species. The effectiveness of conservation strategies and scientific sampling protocols that involve handling and live release can be impacted by the animals’ physiological stress response and post-capture mortality. A complete understanding of elasmobranch corticosteroid response to handling, and how changes in blood biochemistry and acid-base analytes relate to this response and predict post-release survival are currently lacking. We report the results of health assessments in white sharks (N=74) sampled as part of a multidisciplinary study in the Western North Atlantic between 2016 and 2022. Physical exam, hematology, plasma chemistry, protein electrophoresis, and acute phase protein responses were evaluated, and preliminary relative reference intervals created along with descriptive statistics. We additionally report the one-alpha hydroxycorticosterone (1aOHB) response to scientific handling of a subset (N=38) of the study animals, using a monoclonal antibody-based enzyme immune assay (EIA). Relationships between all analytes and biologic data (morphometrics, life-history stage [YOY, juvenile, subadult, adult], season, and region) were explored. We further compared 1aOHB values with blood chemistry, acid-base and blood gas alterations traditionally used to monitor stress response. This study creates a baseline for white shark health assessment in the Western North Atlantic, accounting for intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and contributes to a better understanding of their stress response to scientific handling.

title: Ontogenetic trophic shifts in the pelagic thresher shark Alopias pelagicus from both coasts of Baja California Sur, México
abstract_text: The pelagic thresher shark is an important species in fisheries of Mexico and Ecuador; however, we know few about their biology to recommend management or conservation plans. Understanding the life history of pelagic species is important to ensure their survival. The aim of the present study was to evaluate the trophic ontogeny of Alopias pelagicus from both coasts of Baja California Sur (BCS), Mexico, based on the analysis of stable isotope ratios of carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) of vertebra and muscle. A total of 199 vertebral and 73 muscle samples were analyzed. For Bahía Tortugas (Western coast BCS), mean vertebra isotopic δ15N values were 12.24±1.08‰ (AIR) and δ13C -15.1±0.65‰ (V-PDB); while muscle δ15N values were 16.59±0.66‰ and δ13C -17.13±0.39‰. For Santa Rosalía (Eastern coast BCS), mean vertebra isotopic δ15N values were 14.69±1.18‰ and δ13C -14.23±0.55‰; while muscle δ15N values were 17.81±0.8‰ and δ13C -16.4±0.36‰ δ13C. These results showed higher δ15N values in Santa Rosalía as a result of baseline differences between the two regions; whereas δ13C values were lower in Bahía Tortugas, suggesting a more oceanic behavior (p<0.05). In Santa Rosalía, there were significant differences by sex in vertebrae for δ15N; whereas δ13C showed ontogenetic shifts, indicating that neonates feed on more coastal areas than juveniles or adults (p<0.05). Neither sex nor ontogenetic differences were observed in Bahía Tortugas (p>0.05), evidencing a high overlap between their isotopic niches. The average trophic level obtained for both tissues was ~ 4, which corresponds to a tertiary predator.

title: Personal experience predicts behavioral indicators of tolerance for interactions with sharks and stingrays
abstract_text: Global conservation efforts are critical as the world’s ecosystems are under threat from numerous man-made sources. Humans’ behavioral intentions to support conservancy for diverse species and their habitats are predicated on key intrinsic (cognitions, beliefs, affects) and extrinsic factors. One such critical extrinsic factor which is subject to individual differences is former personal experiences with certain animals, such as previous encounters with different species in the wild. This work examined individuals’ self-reported previous experience with two different animal species (sharks and stingrays) to determine their effects on behavioral expressions of tolerance (i.e., willingness to engage in activities in the water at beach facilities that have experienced confirmed sightings of these species within different timeframes). Results inform the design of instructional and promotional materials intended to promote elasmobranch conservation as well as safety materials (e.g., training, signage) that convey information pertaining to risk at beach and oceanic recreation facilities.

title: Innovative shark mitigation measures tested in Reunion Island towards the reduction of human - shark interactions
abstract_text: Since 2011, the intensity of unprovoked human-shark interaction has dramatically increased on the coast of Reunion Island, with a total of 31 human-shark interactions including 11 fatal shark bites. Most of these interactions occurred within the most popular beaches of the island. The main shark species responsible for these interactions is the bull shark (Carcharhinus leucas). Faced with this unprecedented situation, the French government instituted a ban on all nautical activities around the island and decided to implement a comprehensive strategy to mitigate the risk of human-shark interactions. To ensure the implementation of this strategy, the Reunion Shark Security Centre was officially created in April 2016 and became since June 2020 a French governmental agency. The main objectives of this institution are to coordinate and implement operational mitigation measures contributing to reduce the shark risk in Reunion, as well as to promote mitigation measures reconciling ocean users’ safety and the conservation of marine biodiversity using technological innovations. For the past six years, many innovative mitigation measures have been tested in Reunion waters and other parts of the world. These measures include a highly regulated shark control program using smart drumlines, the creation of new tools to detect potentially dangerous sharks, as well as testing commercially available shark deterrent devices. Thanks to all of these measures, the ban on nautical activities has now been partially lifted in specific areas of the island, with further development to come in the near future.

title: WWF whale shark management strategy in La Paz Bay: an example of conservation

authors.affiliation: RED de Turismo Sustentable y Desarrollo Social A.C.

Comisión Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas (CONANP)

abstract_text: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is an endangered species that seasonally aggregate in the Bay of La Paz, an important feeding ground for juvenile individuals. During the last 20 years, touristic activities involving this species has exponentially increased, growing negative pressure on the animals. Since 2010 The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) in collaboration with the Foundation Telmex Telcel (Alliance WWF-Foundation Telmex Telcel) support the conservation of the whale shark in this region of Mexico. Conservation actions so far implemented include funding local scientists to constantly monitor the presence of the animals and to generate information that is useful in decision-making by the government, encourage education and outreach, support training for guides and captains involved in the touristic activity, habitat improvement through the maintenance of Natural Protected Areas in a post-covid context, and the support to the local authorities in the management of the area of observation. Recently a control center formed by a long distance camara, monitor, and computer was established to guarantee an efficient vigilance of the touristic activity. These actions have achieved a decrease in the shark injuries of 26% since 2016. The collaboration between the civil society organizations such as WWF, private entities, researchers, governs, and local community is essential to achieve the conservation of vulnerable species.

title: Are shark deterrents an effective protection against human-shark interactions?
abstract_text: Over the past few years, the number of human-shark interactions have been on the rise globally. A range of measures meant to mitigate the risk of an interaction has been deployed worldwide, such as preventive fishing or exclusion nets. More recently, the use of a personal shark deterrent has become a popular option for ocean users. Several types of these shark deterrents exist and typically rely on optical, olfactive, magnetic, or electrical stimuli to repel sharks that get too close to the wearer. Until recently, these devices were rarely tested independently and in a robust manner. However, this has now changed and through these recent studies, we learned that not all of these devices were effective in repelling sharks, and that electric shark deterrents are generally the most effective type. However, not all of these deterrents are as effective as the others, and their effectiveness may also vary between shark species. Throughout this presentation, we will go over the existing types of personal shark deterrents to identify their advantages and drawbacks, the results of recent investigations on their effectiveness, but also potential future development for this technology.

title: The Chondrocensus, a platform for engagement and collaborative conservation
abstract_text: The International Census of Chondrichthyans in Human Care (aka the ChondroCensus) launched in 2019 at www.sharksandraysproject.com, as part of the framework of the Association of Zoos & Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals From Extinction (SAFE) Sharks and Rays program. This global census has grown to contain 250 species from 237 facilities across 54 countries world-wide as of May 2022. Besides getting an update count of Chondrichthyans at human care, this platform intends to make this collection of data a truly useful tool for engaging in meaningful, strategic, and collaborative conservation. Stakeholder Teams can complete a survey providing basic husbandry info and add their organizational accrediting body. These data can then be searched by region, organizational accrediting body, genus or species, sex, and the surveyed husbandry criteria. In addition to streamlining periodic reporting required by organizational accrediting bodies, these new features will also anonymously connect stakeholders with each other and with the research community to advance husbandry practices and facilitate collaborative chondrichthyan conservation efforts. Teams always remain anonymous and thus maintain control over their data, as search results are only shown as the number of Teams per ChondroCensus Region. Thus, each stakeholder facility’s Team Coordinator holds the critical role of whether their Team chooses to respond to any requests for connection or information, thereby identifying themselves as stakeholders of the species a search query pertains to.

title: Saving Aussie sharks & rays - the conservation needs of threatened endemic elasmobranchs in Australian waters
abstract_text: Australia is a global hotspot of elasmobranch endemicity, making it a global conservation priority to protect the evolutionary diversity of elasmobranchs. Australia is one of 21 regions in the world containing ‘triple threat hotspots’, regions characterised by the presence of threatened species in high levels of richness, endemicity, and evolutionary distinctiveness. The recent ‘Action Plan for Sharks and Rays 2021’ identifies one third (36%) of Australia’s threatened elasmobranch species being endemic. South-eastern quadrant of Australia (southern Queensland through to eastern Victoria) is a region with a high level of incidence of threatened species as a direct result from commercial fishing. Within this region, there are several state-managed fisheries as well as the federally-managed Southern and Eastern Scalefish and Shark Fishery, Australia’s largest by area and volume. To address these issues and support the recovery of threatened endemic species, I will highlight the opportunities that exist in Australian fisheries management, Australia’s environmental laws, and collaborations with NGOs in linking research to policy. The conservation needs for Australian endemic elasmobranchs are urgent, globally recognised, and forecasted to be successful if appropriate actions are implemented.

title: Using elasmobranch bycatch data to model species distributions and inform conservation management
abstract_text: The short-term socioeconomic impacts of marine spatial conservation measures to the fishing industry, such as the implementation of no-take zones or marine protected areas, often result in these proposals being met with opposition or skepticism, at best. Hence, when spatial conservation measures are implemented to protect a target species or population, they must be strategically located as to maximize their effectiveness, although the field surveys that traditionally underpin this work are time- and resource-intensive. Researchers are therefore increasingly utilizing species distribution models to identify locations of high conservation value. In this study, we aim to establish priority areas for the protection of sharks and rays based on predictions of their distribution in the waters surrounding the Malaysian state of Sabah, in north Borneo. Considering the global decline of elasmobranchs, it is vital for interventions such as spatial conservation management measures to be implemented rapidly and effectively. Here, we use extensive, multi-year bycatch datasets from the Marine Research Foundation for modelling the ranges of species distributions and occurrences of sharks and rays in Sabah. The results of this work will support recommendations for local elasmobranch management measures.

abstract_text: In the last decade, there has been an upsurge in the number of studies that utilise environmental DNA for detecting elasmobranchs, focusing on identifying the presence or absence of species. In this talk, we will explore the application of eDNA methods for long-term and fine-scale monitoring of elasmobranch species. We will present the results from eDNA metabarcoding to assess the diversity of elasmobranchs around a remote atoll in the Chagos Archipelago Marine Protected Area (MPA), showing that eDNA can detect a wide range of elasmobranch species seldom recorded in the MPA. We applied species-specific eDNA methods to assess the distribution of two dominant reef shark species across the archipelago and show that detections were significantly higher around the well-protected atoll of Diego Garcia compared to atolls in the north of the MPA, where detection showed no relationship with concurrent visual surveys or activity hotspots revealed through acoustic telemetry. We infer that populations around the northern atolls have been suppressed by illegal, unregulated and unreported (IUU) fishing activity and that eDNA methods may be limited when investigating species at low population density. In addition, we will showcase how species-specific eDNA methods to investigate the seasonal presence of the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) and thornback ray (Raja clavata) over the course of a year in Wales. Using both case studies, we emphasise the potential of eDNA methods for elasmobranch monitoring and highlight areas of further research that will be required as they move beyond detection validation into real-world conservation applications.

abstract_text: The movements of stingrays have often been quantified over small localized scales however, it still remains largely unknown whether species display site fidelity or dispersal and to what extent they may connect coastal habitats. This information is vital to inform population dynamics, ecological roles and best management practices for this threatened faunal group. Blue stingrays Dasyatis chrysonota, endemic to southern Africa, are hypothesized to move from shallow inshore habitats to deeper offshore waters during winter, making them a model species to investigate these large-scale movement questions. Twenty-seven individuals were monitored using the Acoustic Tracking Array Platform (ATAP – a nation-wide network of acoustic receivers) for up to 4.5 years. Individuals displayed site fidelity to defined regions of the coast with the majority of detections being recorded in the shallow bay/coastal shelf they were tagged in. However, important movement corridors linking different habitats were identified (inshore vs offshore and coastal bay vs coastal shelf habitats). Modelling highlighted this habitat use was influenced by month and temperature, with individuals displaying restricted movements to the shallow bay habitat in summer when deeper waters were colder. The large collaborative nature of the ATAP allowed for the monitoring of a benthic stingray across large spatial scales (hundreds of kilometres) for the first time, challenging preconceived notions that small undulatory batoids cannot travel large distances (many individuals travelled up to 200 km). Lastly, the current Marine Protected Area zonation may be insufficient to protect blue stingrays from further population declines in South Africa.

The video survey recorded two shark species, the blacktip reef shark Carcharhinus melanopterus and the Arabian carpet shark Chiloscyllium arabicum, two shark like rays, halavi guitarfish Glaucostegus halavi and the giant guitarfish Rhynchobatus djiddensis and six ray species, the honeycomb stingray Himantura uarnak, the leopard whipray Himantura leoparda, the pink whipray Pateobatis fai, the cowtail stingray Pastinachus sp., the Arabic whipray Maculabatis arabica and the eagle ray Aetobatus ocellatus. abstract_text: The EMREP project aims to develop technology that integrates electronic reporting (ER) and electronic monitoring (EM) technologies to create an integrated, onboard, monitoring and reporting solution (iEMR) for commercial fishing fleets. As part of the project, the iEMR system is being tested onboard a Portuguese bottom-trawl fishing vessel. It provides a combined tool for the collection of commercial and scientific fishing data, focusing on finding ways to reduce elasmobranch bycatch. The iEMR system makes use of the Olrac fishing eLog system, presently used on hundreds of vessels across fisheries worldwide. The Olrac eLog uses advanced data and communication technologies to facilitate a more accurate, reliable, and efficient approach to the collection, reporting and management of commercial fishing data. Its main advantage is its ability to record data during fishing operations, which can then be used to compile and send out reports needed by a wide range of interested and permitted recipients (commercial, scientific, compliance and management, etc.). The system is also linked to a web-server where data and images from many units across an entire fleet can be stored, analyzed and viewed by different permitted recipients. This iEMR solution provides an innovative and holistic solution to the ever-increasing demand for high quality data within the field of fish resource management. The system is simple to use, allows for data of all kinds (numerical, lookups, free text and images) to be collected and reported and thus transforms every vessel using it into a reliable data collection platform.

title: Integrating distribution and behavioural data from drones to study fine-scale habitat use of stingrays in intertidal flats
abstract_text: Stingrays are ubiquitous in marine ecosystems across the world and perform a variety of functional roles that support ecosystem health and stability. Coastal intertidal flats provide productive nursery habitats for juvenile rays, making them key areas to target for conservation and management of at-risk species. However, little research has been dedicated to studying distribution patterns or behavioural ecology of juvenile rays in estuaries, limiting our capacity to identify critical ray habitats or understand the roles of different species within them. From 2020-2022, we conducted observational surveys of ray communities across intertidal estuary flats in North Queensland using unmanned aerial drones (UAVs). Our aim was to evaluate fine-scale habitat use patterns by integrating spatio-temporal distribution and behavioural data. We found species compositions varied across locations based on their spatial features, and there was evidence of species-specific habitat partitioning within sites. Daily movements of rays were generally characterized by individuals moving into the upper intertidal flats during rising and high tidal periods and returning to subtidal zones during ebb and low periods. Incorporating behaviours showed that foraging may be a primary driver for these movements, and species-specific behaviours may further contribute to differential habitat use. In some locations, ray activity was evidenced by dense, patchy clusters of feeding pits, suggesting there is fine-scale variability for where feeding occurs within larger habitat areas. Overall, making comparisons beyond single-site contexts broadened our understanding about spatio-temporal distributions of rays in intertidal estuaries. More behavioural studies will be useful for linking specific activities to ecological functions.

title: The elephant in the room: assessing the foraging ecology of Callorhinchus milii across Australia and New Zealand
abstract_text: The functions of mesopredators often overlooked, despite their role as ecologically-vital trophic links. Elephant fish, Callorhinchus milii, are presumed to be a regionally-important mesopredator across southern Australia and New Zealand, yet little is known about their ecology. We investigated the foraging ecology of C. milii across two locations in Australia (Bass Strait and Robe) and New Zealand (Southeast and Southwest) using stomach content, stable isotope and fatty acid analysis to enable the assessment of spatial variations in feeding across different spatial scales. Callorhinchus milii mostly fed on preys from non-complex habitat, although diet of C. milli varied between all sampled locations, with differences in muscle being primarily driven by higher δ13C and 16:0 within Robe and Bass Strait summer identifying more pelagic foraging. Lower δ13C and higher 20:5ω3 within Bass Strait winter, Southeast and Southwest New Zealand identified non-complex demersal foraging. In addition to similar ẟ15N, C. milii within Bass Strait summer and winter, and Robe predominantly fed on polychaetes (0.785), and teleost + cephalopods (0.137), and Southeast New Zealand mostly feeds on polychaetes (0.660) annually. Within liver, the same trends were seen, although lower δ13C and higher 18:1ω9 within Bass Strait summer, and lower δ13C and higher 22:6ω3 within Southeast New Zealand identified more deep-sea foraging. With similar ẟ15N, C. milii within Bass Strait summer and winter predominantly fed on polychaetes (0.423) and teleost + cephalopods (0.132), Robe on polychaetes (0.755), and teleost + cephalopods (0.132), and Southeast New Zealand on teleost + cephalopods (0.504), and crustaceans (0.188) seasonally. Our findings improve our understanding of C. milii trophic ecology, and chimaera ecology more broadly, for which minimal information is currently available.

title: Trophic niche overlap and segregation among elasmobranch predators in a unique island environment
abstract_text: The processes that allow co-occurring predators to avoid competitive exclusion is the subject of many ecological questions, with resource partitioning the most widely accepted process enabling coexistence. The degree to which predators overlap or divide resources can be explored by quantifying their trophic niche, which is a multidimensional space governed by a species’ prey preferences, habitat, and trophic level. Here, we use fatty acids and stable isotopes to quantify trophic niche width and overlap among tiger (Galeocerdo cuvier), dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus), and Galapagos sharks (Carcharhinus galapagensis) from Norfolk Island, an isolated offshore island 800 nm off the east coast of Australia, and determine the variation in overlap across three years. Results reveal substantial overlap between dusky and Galapagos sharks but segregation from the tiger sharks, with all three species contracting and expanding their trophic niches among years but remaining segregated. Changes in trophic niches among years highlights predator ability to adapt to fluctuating resources. Yet, niche overlaps between species remained consistent, indicating stable predatory role and competitive pressure. Temporal variability in the feeding ecology of marine predators is an important component of species’ ecology to consider when managing populations, since species that can contract or expand their niche are better able to adapt to environmental change.

title: The diet of tiger sharks on Norfolk Island inferred from biochemical markers
abstract_text: Norfolk Island is a small island in the Pacific Ocean, ~1,400 km east of Australia that supports a broad diversity of temperate and tropical marine life, including many shark and pelagic fish species. In particular, Norfolk Island is home to a large aggregation of mature female tiger sharks Galeocerdo cuvier, with unknown diet, foraging ecology, and movement patterns. While the reliability of this aggregation makes Norfolk Island an ideal site to uncover the ecology of these top predators, no work to date has quantitatively explored what tiger sharks consume in this region, or how long they spend in these coastal waters. The local community has also raised concerns about the disposal of cow offal, rubbish, and fish frames, which are presumed to attract the tiger sharks that are observed feeding at the disposal sight. Here, we used stable isotopes and fatty acids from 60 tiger shark blood and muscle samples collected in 2020 and 2021 to quantify the role of cow offal in the diet of these generalist predators. Despite the frequent observation of tiger sharks consuming cow offal, isotope models suggest that local seabirds are the predominate prey source for these large tiger sharks sampled around Norfolk Island.

abstract_text: Quantifying the trophic role of an animal is key to understanding its ecology and ecosystem function. Despite the regular occurrence of sawsharks in Australian temperate fisheries, there remains limited information on their trophic ecology or niche. We used fatty acid and stable isotope profiles, along with stomach content analysis to investigate the trophic ecology of two sympatric species of sawsharks, the common sawshark (Pristiophorus cirratus) and southern sawshark (Pristiophorus nudipinnis) in south-eastern Australia. C, N and S isotopic analysis of sawshark muscle revealed that P. nudipinnis fed at a higher trophic level than P. cirratus. Stomach contents also showed that Pristiophorus nudipinnis fed on a mix of benthic and pelagic species while P. cirratus foraged predominantly on benthic species. This bentho-pelagic partitioning between species was further supported by fatty acid analysis where P. nudipinnis fatty acid profiles had higher levels of tracers associated with dinoflagellate basal sources (16:1/16:0, 22:6ω3) than P. cirratus, indicating a reliance on pelagic food webs. These data suggest that these two sympatric species may display resource partitioning to avoid competition. Furthermore, that these mesopredators play a substantial role in the pelagic food web which was previously unknown and demonstrates the value of incorporating multiple biochemical tracers to provide a comprehensive representation of an animals trophic ecology.

title: Olfactory capabilities of mako shark and blind shark assessed using anatomical and molecular methods
abstract_text: Sharks have been associated with an infamously powerful sense of smell. However, research on the sensory biology of this taxa is still scarce, although it is critical for the development of more selective fishing gear and more efficient shark deterrents. Notably, the selective pressures that shape the olfactory organs of sharks and their effect on olfactory capabilities are poorly understood. Here, a multidisciplinary approach combining anatomical and molecular techniques was used to characterise the olfactory organs of two shark species: the pelagic, shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and the benthic blind shark (Brachaelurus waddi). The total sensory surface area of the olfactory organs—a traditional proxy of olfactory capabilities—is relatively larger in I. oxyrinchus due to greater coverage of sensory epithelium and more extensive secondary folding of the lamellae. However, examination of the de novo-assembled olfactory transcriptomes reveals a more diversified olfactory receptor repertoire in B. waddi. These findings suggest that sharks may rely on different olfactory strategies (i.e. more extensive olfactory organs and/or more diversified receptor repertoires) that may be related to the characteristics of the water flow within their olfactory organs, their ecological needs (trade-off sensitivity over diversity of odorants detected) and/or phylogeny. Consequently, these findings indicate that multidisciplinary studies considering the anatomical and molecular traits of the olfactory system of sharks are required to fully comprehend the olfactory capabilities of this group.

title: Feeding ontogeny of the silky shark, Carcharhinus falciformis, in the Eastern Tropical Pacific of Colombia
abstract_text: The trophic patterns of predators are the result of differences in habitat use and the relationship with the environment and their prey during their life cycle. The study of the feeding ontogeny of large predators is difficult due to their high mobility, which leaves part of their life poorly understood. This study describes the trophic ontogeny of Carcharhinus falciformis in the Colombian Pacific. Vertebrae from 12 specimens were analyzed, obtaining a total of 61 vertebral collagen samples grouped into four maturity stages and eight age groups. The d13C values indicate that the different categories of C. falciformis makes use of coastal and oceanic zones (-17.8‰ to -14.0‰). The d13C and d15N values (9.4‰ to 12.4‰) suggest that C. falciformis is a species that can occupy different trophic positions (PTs: 3.4-5.6). Isotopic values estimated in C. falciformis show small ontogenetic changes in habitat use and prey consumption that were related to age and sex. Additionally, C. falciformis showed narrow (SEAC: 0.14‰2) and broad (SEAC: 3.16‰2) isotopic niches in the different categories, due to a high trophic interaction between them. In conclusion, C. falciformis shows a greater preference for oceanic areas, indicating that the oceanic islands of the southeastern Pacific may be important feeding sites, and Colombian mangroves may be used as potential breeding areas. In addition, this species reflects ontogenetic changes in area use and prey consumption, which leads the species to occupy different trophic positions and show changes in feeding-related to body growth/age, as well as two sex-related migratory patterns.

title: Angel shark (Squatinidae: Squatina squatina, Squatina oculata, Squatina aculeata) records, age validation techniques, and conservation strategies for Turkey
abstract_text: Three species of angel sharks are distributed in the Mediterranean Sea (Squatina squatina, Squatina oculata and Squatina aculaeta), all of which are critically endangered. They only remain now in a few pockets surrounding the Mediterranean basin, and mostly at alarmingly low levels. These species have considerable knowledge gaps relating to their age and growth. This study experimented three ageing techniques on Squatina squatina which were unable to yield clear results, due to a lack of reference data, but can be used to improve future studies. Since 2018, their catch and landing have become prohibited both in the European Union and Turkey, hence fishers no longer report these catches in fear of penalties. Therefore, each angel shark record is extremely important in understanding their distribution, habitat use and remaining hotspots with the aim of protecting their last refuges. This study adds seven new angel shark records for Turkish waters, three Squatina squatina, three Squatina aculeata and one Squatina oculata, confirming all three species are still currently found in the region and denoting parts of the Aegean Sea as remaining hotspots. The presence of all three species should warrant immediate conservation actions to improve their prospects and protect them from localized extinction.

abstract_text: One of the main components of effective fisheries management is post-capture survival rates. Globally, Rhino rays are the most threatened among all vertebrates, and bycatch poses a significant challenge to their conservation. Moreover, most species are endemic to areas where inspection is scarce and fisheries management is difficult to implement (i.e., low and middle-low-income countries). In these situations, recovery plans based on fishers' participatory management through bycatch release is a promising strategy. However, it is necessary to understand how species respond to capture as well as how they recover from it. The present study aimed to investigate the recovery capacity of incidentally captured Shortnose Guitarfish through the analysis of energy markers (β-hydroxybutyrate and glucose) and circulating levels of lactate. Zapteryx brevirostris captured by artisanal fleets were donated to our research group and kept fasted and monitored for 120 hours before release. Blood samples were collected shortly after capture and right before release. The results indicated that all guitarfish depleted their β-hydroxybutyrate reserves, concomitant to glucose mobilization and high levels of circulating lactate upon capture, indicating allostatic overload and lactic acidosis. After 120 hours, all subjects were able to recover their β-hydroxybutyrate stores, and both glucose and lactate levels were significantly lower. The results indicate great recovery potential in Z. brevirostris - strongly affected by bycatch despite its low selling price. The species is currently listed as "Endangered" globally, and recovery plans based on bycatch release proved to be effective based on their recovery capacity.

title: Using Drones to Assess Volitional Swimming Kinematics of Manta Ray Behaviors in the Wild
abstract_text: Drones have become increasingly popular tools to study marine megafauna but are underutilized in batoid research. We used drones to collect video data of manta ray (Mobula cf. birostris) swimming and assessed behavior-specific kinematics in Kinovea, a semi-automated point-tracking software. We describe a ‘resting’ behavior of mantas making use of strong currents in man-made inlets in addition to known ‘traveling’ and ‘feeding’ behaviors. No significant differences were found between the swimming speed of traveling and feeding behaviors, although feeding mantas had a significantly higher wingbeat frequency than traveling mantas. Resting mantas swam at a significantly slower speed and wingbeat frequency, suggesting that they were continuously swimming with the minimum effort required to maintain position and buoyancy. Swimming speed and wingbeat frequency of traveling and feeding behaviors overlapped, which could point to other factors such as prey availability and a transitional behavior, influencing how manta rays swim. Additionally, we present preliminary swimming kinematics data of a ‘surface feeding’ behavior. As ‘surface feeding’ was only observed in larger, and possibly mature, individuals, future research should investigate any ontogenetic separation of behaviors and kinematics. These baseline swimming kinematic data have valuable applications to other emerging technologies in manta ray research.

title: Behavioural patterns in marine predators - how does reef habitat complexity affect the distribution and habitat use of reef sharks?

authors.affiliation: University of Western Australia; Marine Futures Lab

abstract_text: Increases in shark fishing and the frequency of climate disturbance events in the last decades have led to a global decline in reef shark populations and degradation of the coral reefs they inhabit. A recent study documented that sharks were absent from 20% of the 371 reefs surveyed (MacNeil et al., 2020). Indian Ocean areas were highlighted as in crucial need of protection and were identified as having great potential to implement shark-based management approaches. The aim of this research is to understand how coral reef complexity influences shark habitat use at fine scales. I will use seabed Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS), acoustic telemetry, faecal DNA (fDNA) swabbing, and coral and fish diversity and biomass monitoring datasets to document the fine-scale distribution and habitat use patterns of three reef shark species, the grey reef shark (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos), blacktip reef shark (Carcharinus melanopterus), and sharptooth lemon shark (Negaprion acutidens). Their behaviour will then be correlated to reef complexity acquired from 3D structure from motion (SfM) photogrammetry modelling to understand how future reef homogenization may affect shark behaviour. The distribution of sharks is frequently studied at large spatial scales over 100s to 1000s of kilometres. My research, focused on small scale distributions across 100s to 1000s of metres and the drivers of these patterns with respect to habitat complexity and prey availability, is a novel and conservation-relevant addition to the existing literature. The outcomes of this research can be utilized by practitioners across the Indian Ocean and Indo-Pacific region and will not only further our understanding of the intrinsic fine scale behaviour of these predators, but aid in the planning, implementation and management of marine protected areas (MPAs) in the region.

title: Drivers of ray sightings on baited remote underwater videos in the tropical Western Atlantic Ocean
abstract_text: Rays are threatened globally by overfishing, habitat loss, climate change, and pollution. In the tropical Western Atlantic Ocean, rays are part of artisanal, commercial, and recreational fisheries, yet management is sparse and hindered by a lack species-specific population data. Drivers of ray abundance and habitat use in the region are not well-understood. To address these knowledge gaps, we compared ray sightings per unit effort (MaxN) across gradients of human pressure (market gravity), fishing regulations, fishing gear, predator abundance (shark MaxN), and environmental variables using a baited remote underwater video station (BRUVS) dataset provided by Global FinPrint. Over 3500 BRUVS were set on coral reefs in 17 countries from the United States to Brazil that detected at least nine ray species (Aetobatus narinari, Hypanus americanus, H. berthalutzae, H. marianae, Mobula sp., Narcine bancroftii, Pseudobatos lentiginosus, Styracura schmardae, Urobatis jamaicensis). Factors influencing MaxN of the most common ray species and pooled MaxN of all rays will be presented. We will discuss the implications of our results for local and regional management.

abstract_text: Sharks are declining rapidly because of their vulnerable life histories and the direct and indirect impacts of fishing and habitat modification. For this reason, they are among the most endangered animals in the ocean. Meanwhile, they are also among the most poorly quantified groups of vertebrates on the planet, as basic information on abundance, distribution, and life-history is lacking for most species. Hence there is an urgent need to collect and analyze data on sharks to increase our understanding of their ecology, develop effective conservation actions, and reverse their loss. Here we show how crowdsourcing, web data-mining, and machine learning techniques can fill this critical information gap. We are building the largest database of shark occurrence records by implementing sharkPulse, a modular crowd-sourcing platform that combines smartphone and web applications, social network and website crawling, and image analysis to fill knowledge gaps in global shark populations. We will illustrate the architecture of this platform and show how hundreds of thousands of online images can be sourced and transformed into shark sightings. We explore the opportunities from crowdsourcing, artificial intelligence, big-data approaches, and social network mining to quickly and cost-effectively fill major knowledge gaps in shark distribution and characterize their status and drivers of decline. We also list a series of challenges that need to be addressed to efficiently source this information continuously and produce efficient and real-time monitoring of global shark populations.

title: Shark detection and classification with machine learning

authors.affiliation: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

abstract_text: Suitable shark conservation depends on well-informed population assessments. Direct methods such as scientific surveys and fisheries monitoring are adequate for defining population statuses, but species-specific indices of abundance and distribution coming from these sources are rare for most shark species. We can rapidly fill these information gaps by boosting media-based remote monitoring efforts with machine learning and automation. We created a database of 53,345 shark images covering 219 species of sharks, and packaged object-detection and image classification models into a Shark Detector bundle. The Shark Detector recognizes and classifies sharks from videos and images using transfer learning and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We applied these models to common data-generation approaches of sharks: collecting occurrence records from photographs taken by the public or citizen scientists, processing baited remote camera footage and online videos, and data-mining Instagram. We examined the accuracy of each model and tested genus and species prediction correctness as a result of training data quantity. The Shark Detector can classify 47 species pertaining to 26 genera. It sorted heterogeneous datasets of images sourced from Instagram with 91% accuracy and classified species with 70% accuracy. It located sharks in baited remote footage and YouTube videos with 89% accuracy, and classified located subjects to the species level with 69% accuracy. All data-generation methods were processed without manual interaction. As media-based remote monitoring appears to dominate methods for observing sharks in nature, we developed an open-source Shark Detector to facilitate common identification applications. Prediction accuracy of the software pipeline increases as more images are added to the training dataset. We provide public access to the software on our GitHub page.

title: Seasonal aggregations and movements of blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) at Cabo Pulmo National Park, Gulf of California, Mexico

abstract_text: The Angelshark (Squatina squatina) was formerly common across the East Atlantic and Mediterranean Seas, but has undergone dramatic declines over the last 50 years. Despite this reduction, the Canary Islands remain a uniquely large stronghold for the species, where Angelsharks can still be observed frequently. Protection of Angelsharks in the Canary Islands is therefore of vital importance to ensure the survival of the species, as threats such as habitat loss and accidental capture in fisheries still impact Angelsharks in these waters. In 2019, Angelsharks were listed in the Spanish Endangered Species List for Canary Islands waters, under the category “In danger of extinction”. In accordance with this listing, it was required that a Recovery Plan be developed, including the delineation of areas relevant to the conservation of the Angelsharks (ARCAs), where specific measures should be implemented. Using this data, alongside current knowledge of Angelshark ecology, ASP:CI were able to determine specific criteria to delineate ARCAs in the Canary Islands. title: Sawfish spotters fill data gaps critical for protection in Queensland, Australia
abstract_text: In Australia, effective management of critically endangered sawfishes is a difficult task, in part due to remaining habitat being extremely remote and expensive to reach. Since the federal recovery plan was put in place in 2015, field investigation in Queensland has been limited to a select few river systems, not allowing for a full-scale species distribution assessment. In 2017, Sharks And Rays Australia launched a public sightings campaign targeted at recreational fishers to fill knowledge gaps in population abundance and spatial ecology. Since then, over 950 submissions have been received Australia-wide from members of the public. Data from Queensland encounters reported to have taken place between 1998 and 2022 were analysed, representing equal temporal distribution before and after federal protection. Sighting locations were analysed for association with commercial and recreational fishing pressure and environmental protection measures. Size and year of capture were shown to be negatively correlated, even over a relatively short time span of 20 years. Condition of the animal also varied with species, size and method of capture, indicating a varied impact on sawfishes through different fishing methods. This study provides first insights into key habitat for different life history stages on the Queensland coast since becoming federally protected. Additionally, findings highlight the importance of citizen science as a reliable data source, and a platform for the direct involvement of the recreational fishing community in protecting critically endangered species.

abstract_text: As the popularity of recreational scuba diving grows, so does the will of scuba divers to contribute towards the protection and conservation of the marine environment. This growth has been accompanied by the establishment of a citizen science movement aimed to engage and recruit scuba divers in data collection for research. This innovative tool has been used in the Canary Islands to gather data on the Critically Endangered Angelshark (Squatina squatina) through an annual event named Count the Angels (CTA), which has been completed for four years (2018-2021). The CTA event is organised under the direction and supervision of the Angel Shark Project: Canary Islands. During four days, participating dive centres and clubs carry out two coordinated dives at scheduled hours and register specific data, including Angelshark sightings. The last CTA event was held from the 4 to the 7 of December 2021, with a total of 37 participating dive centres and clubs, 107 dives registered and a total of 166 Angelsharks recorded throughout five of the Canary Islands. The collected data has allowed different analysis including shark size and sex ratio, behaviour patterns, encounter probability and abundance estimates for the different islands. This unique and growing event is an example of how citizen science can be a valuable tool not only to support Angelshark research, but also as a mechanism to create awareness and engage scuba divers towards the conservation of a Critically Endangered species. CTA events were funded by Shark Conservation Fund, Disney Conservation Fund and WWF Netherlands.

abstract_text: Rhino rays are facing a global conservation crisis. These 67 species (families Pristidae (Sawfishes), Glaucostegidae (Giant Guitarfishes), Rhinidae (Wedgefishes), Rhinobatidae (Guitarfishes), and Trygonorrhinidae (Banjo Rays)) have limited productivity making them extremely susceptible to overexploitation. Rhino rays face an uncertain future with 68.7% considered threatened with extinction according to the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. We focus on understanding the status and uncovering the drivers behind their exploitation in four data-poor countries: India, Mauritania, Senegal, and Sri Lanka. These species richness or endemicity hotspots are data-poor in terms of fisheries, have some of the poorest coastal communities, and species’ distributions overlap with intense and increasing fishing pressure. Data were collected by interviewing fishers and traders to record historical knowledge and current perceptions, as well as landing site surveys to collect data on species and assess how fisheries impact them. Results suggest that species exploitation is not always driven by the fin trade but also by demand for their meat, often consumed locally. Landing site surveys indicate a low abundance of species while fishers describe historical high abundances, indicative of potential localized extinctions going unnoticed. The complexities in understanding these fisheries at the local scale highlight that conventional fisheries management measures are unlikely to yield results, especially when governance is weak in terms of enforcement and policy implementation. Adaptive local actions are needed with solutions based on fisher engagement to ensure their livelihoods and nutritional needs are taken into consideration while identifying potential mitigation measures or solutions to reduce demand.
